stem: An 11-year-old boy has three weeks of right thigh pain and warmth with low-grade fever. X-ray shows a lytic lesion in the mid-shaft of the femur with layered periosteal reaction. A biopsy is taken.
oneliner: 11M + thigh pain + low-grade fever + mid-shaft lytic femur lesion + layered periosteal reaction → which histologic pattern?

options.A: Sheets of small uniform round blue cells with scant cytoplasm and no matrix
options.B: Spindle cells directly producing pink bone matrix
options.C: Cells with vacuolated scalloped nuclei and fat droplets
options.D: Pale cells with grooved nuclei mixed with eosinophils
options.E: Sheets of cells with eccentric nuclei and clock-face chromatin

whyNot.B: **Osteoid production** defines osteosarcoma, usually at the metaphysis with a sunburst pattern
whyNot.C: **Lipoblasts** mean liposarcoma, a soft-tissue tumor of adults
whyNot.D: **Langerhans cells with eosinophils** (CD1a) make a punched-out lesion, usually skull or flat bone, without layered periosteum and fever
whyNot.E: **Plasma cells** mean myeloma, a disease of older adults, not an 11-year-old

why: **Ewing sarcoma** arises in the **diaphysis** of children and shows **sheets of small, uniform round cells** with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and **no matrix**. **Onion-skin periosteum** and fever mimic osteomyelitis; it carries **t(11;22) EWS-FLI1**.

idea.rule: Diaphyseal bone tumor in a child with small round blue cells and no matrix is Ewing sarcoma.
also: Cells are PAS positive from glycogen and CD99 positive
Neuroblastoma, lymphoma and rhabdomyosarcoma are other small round blue cell tumors
Responds to chemotherapy; arises from neuroectodermal-type cells

stem: A 52-year-old man wakes with a hot, swollen, exquisitely tender first metatarsophalangeal joint after a weekend of heavy drinking and red meat. Serum urate is raised. Fluid aspirated from the joint is examined under compensated polarized light.
oneliner: 52M + hot swollen first MTP after heavy drinking + raised urate + aspirate under polarized light → which crystal appearance?
ask: Which crystal appearance is most likely in the aspirate?

options.A: Rhomboid crystals that look blue when parallel to the compensator axis
options.B: Needle-shaped crystals that look blue when parallel to the compensator axis
options.C: Envelope-shaped crystals typical of calcium oxalate deposition
options.D: Flat plates with notched corners typical of cholesterol
options.E: Needle-shaped crystals that look yellow when parallel to the compensator axis

whyNot.A: **Rhomboid, positively birefringent** crystals are calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout), usually in an older patient's knee; here the clue is **raised urate** with a first MTP attack
whyNot.B: Right shape but wrong sign: **blue when parallel** is positive birefringence, which urate does not show
whyNot.C: Calcium oxalate forms **envelope** crystals in renal failure or oxalate disease, not in a **urate-driven first MTP attack**
whyNot.D: Cholesterol **plates** occur in chronic effusions such as long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, not in an **acute attack with raised urate**

answer: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis)
why: **Raised urate** with acute **first MTP monoarthritis** is gout, and the aspirate shows **monosodium urate** crystals. They are **needle-shaped** and **negatively birefringent**: **yellow when parallel** to the compensator axis, blue when perpendicular.

idea.rule: Urate = needles, negative birefringence, yellow when parallel; pyrophosphate = rhomboids, positive birefringence, blue when parallel.
also: Yellow Parallel, Negative = urate; Blue Parallel, Positive = pyrophosphate
Tophi are chalky urate deposits with the same needle crystals
Uric acid stones in the urine are radiolucent on plain film

stem: A 25-year-old man falls on his outstretched hand and has severe wrist pain with numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers. On the lateral wrist x-ray the distal radius is intact and the capitate stays in line with the radius, but the carpal bone that normally sits between them has slipped in front of the radius with its concave surface turned toward the palm.
oneliner: 25M + fall on outstretched hand + numb thumb, index, middle fingers + lateral film: intact radius, capitate in line, middle carpal bone in front of radius, concavity facing palm → which sign?

whyNot.B: A widened scapholunate **gap on the frontal view**; this is a **lateral** film with a carpal bone displaced toward the palm
whyNot.C: Flexion collapse of a **fractured scaphoid**; here no fracture is described, and the displaced bone is the one **between radius and capitate**
whyNot.D: Dorsal angulation of a **fractured distal radius** (Colles); his **distal radius is intact**
whyNot.E: A cortical ring of a flexed scaphoid on the **frontal view**; this is a **lateral** film of a different, central carpal bone

why: On the lateral film the **lunate** normally sits in the radius and cradles the capitate like a cup. In an **anterior (volar) lunate dislocation** it tips out toward the palm with its **concavity facing forward** while the **capitate stays in line with the radius**: the **spilled teacup**. The displaced lunate presses on the **median nerve** in the carpal tunnel.

idea.rule: On a lateral wrist film the radius, lunate and capitate line up like stacked cups; a lunate tipped toward the palm with the capitate still aligned is the spilled teacup of lunate dislocation.
also: Perilunate dislocation: the capitate displaces dorsally while the lunate stays with the radius
Terry Thomas sign: scapholunate ligament injury on the frontal view
Acute carpal tunnel syndrome can follow a lunate dislocation

stem: A 19-year-old man gets painful muscle cramps and weakness within minutes of sprinting, and once passed dark urine afterward. If he rests briefly, he can continue exercising more easily. His fasting glucose is normal. On a forearm ischemic exercise test, lactate does not rise. A muscle biopsy is stained.
oneliner: 19M + cramps and weakness minutes into sprinting + dark urine after + feels better after short rest + normal fasting glucose + no lactate rise → which biopsy finding?
ask: Which biopsy finding is most likely?

options.A: Ragged red fibers with abnormal mitochondria on Gomori trichrome
options.B: Lipid droplets accumulating within type I muscle fibers
options.D: Perifascicular atrophy with a CD4 T-cell infiltrate
options.E: Absent dystrophin staining with fibrofatty replacement of fibers

whyNot.A: **Mitochondrial myopathy** causes fatigue and lactic acidosis, so lactate would rise on exercise; his **lactate does not rise**
whyNot.B: A **lipid** storage myopathy (carnitine or CPT II) causes cramps after **prolonged** exercise or fasting; he cramps within **minutes of sprinting** and glucose is normal
whyNot.D: **Dermatomyositis** gives proximal weakness with skin rash, not **exercise-triggered cramps with myoglobinuria**
whyNot.E: **Duchenne dystrophy** is a progressive boyhood weakness with very high CK at rest, not **episodic exertional cramps with a second wind**

answer: Excess subsarcolemmal glycogen (PAS positive) with absent myophosphorylase staining
why: Cramps, **myoglobinuria** and a **flat lactate** curve on forearm exercise, with a **second wind**, are classic for **McArdle disease** (muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency). Glycogen cannot be broken down, so it **accumulates under the sarcolemma** and stains **PAS positive** while **myophosphorylase stain is absent**.

idea.rule: No lactate rise with exercise plus a second wind and myoglobinuria means muscle glycogen cannot be mobilised.
also: Blood glucose stays normal because the liver isoform is intact
Second wind comes from fatty acids and blood glucose delivered to muscle
